The Readiness of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) to Adopt AI-Based Accounting Systems in Pakistan
abstract: This study investigates the readiness of Small and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) in Pakistan to adopt Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based accounting systems. Despite the transformative potential of AI in automating financial processes and improving reporting accuracy, adoption remains limited in the Pakistani SME sector. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) and the Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) theory as theoretical anchors, this research employs a mixed-methods approach, integrating a structured survey (n = 312) administered to SME owners, financial managers, and accountants across Lahore, Karachi, and Islamabad with qualitative in-depth interviews (n = 18). Structural Equation Modelling (SEM) was used for quantitative analysis. Results reveal that perceived usefulness (β = 0.47, p < 0.001), digital infrastructure quality (β = 0.38, p < 0.01), and top management support (β = 0.33, p < 0.01) are the most significant predictors of AI adoption readiness, while financial constraints and low digital literacy constitute the primary barriers. The study contributes novel empirical insights into AI technology adoption in the context of an emerging economy and offers actionable recommendations for policymakers, financial regulators, and SME managers. This paper advances the discourse on digital financial transformation within developing markets. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; SMEs; AI-Based Accounting; Technology Adoption; Pakistan; TAM; Digital Transformation; Emerging Economies
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Role of Generative AI in Small and Medium Enterprises: Opportunities & Challenges
abstract: AbstractSmall and Medium Enterprises (SMEs) are essential contributors to global economic growth, innovation, and employment, yet they face unique barriers in their digital transformation journeys. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) presents a significant opportunity for SMEs to enhance productivity, strengthen customer engagement, and build competitive advantage. Applications of AI in areas such as process automation, predictive analytics, and personalised services offer potential for innovation and long-term growth. However, adoption remains limited due to persistent challenges, including high implementation costs, shortage of technical expertise, organisational resistance to change, and cybersecurity vulnerabilities. This paper synthesises findings from recent studies (2022–2025) to examine both the opportunities and challenges associated with AI integration in SMEs. The review highlights that while awareness of AI technologies is rising, practical implementation is slow, indicating a critical awareness–adoption gap. To bridge this divide, SMEs must adopt phased and strategic approaches, supported by employee training, enabling policy incentives, and human-centred AI practices that balance technological potential with ethical considerations.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption, Implementation Barriers, and Business Impact in Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: The empirical and conceptual research on artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that was published between 2019 and 2025 is compiled in this systematic literature review. This evaluation incorporates information from three main research domains: AI applications in business operations, adoption enablers and barriers, and organizational performance results. It is based on fifty peer-reviewed articles that were found through searches of Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore. Results show that in order to improve customer service, marketing automation, and operational efficiency, SMEs primarily use machine learning, natural language processing, and chatbot technologies. While financial limitations, a lack of skills, and insufficient digital infrastructure continue to be obstacles, top management support, technical preparedness, and staff capability emerge as crucial organizational facilitators. Although adoption rates are still concentrated among larger organizations, AI adoption is correlated with quantifiable increases in operational efficiency, cost reduction, customer retention, and innovation performance. There are clear regional differences, with rising nations in Latin America and Asia spearheading adoption despite more limited resources. Significant research gaps about long-term sustainability, contextual differences among developing economies, ethical governance frameworks, and the efficacy of support interventions are identified by the review. To promote inclusive, responsible AI integration in SMEs, our findings highlight the necessity of customized implementation strategies, focused capacity-building initiatives, encouraging legislative frameworks, and multi-stakeholder cooperation. For practitioners, governments, and researchers looking to close the gap in AI adoption and uncover revolutionary potential for small businesses worldwide, this paper offers practical ideas.

title: Artificial Intelligence Adoption Among Small and Medium Enterprises in the United Kingdom: Entrepreneurial Opportunities, Project Management Implications and the Productivity Paradox
abstract: The study examined the accelerating adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the United Kingdom during the 2025-2026 period, with particular attention to the entrepreneurial opportunities that AI creates and the project management implications for firms navigating digital transformation. Problem statement: While the UK Government's AI Opportunities Action Plan and its January 2026 progress update signal aggressive state-backed investment in national AI infrastructure, adoption at the SME level remains fragmented and yields limited financial return. Only twelve per cent of AI-using UK firms report AI-attributable revenue increases, revealing a persistent "productivity-profit gap." Methodology: The study adopts a systematic narrative review of secondary data, drawing on primary UK Government publications, industry benchmark reports, and peer-reviewed working papers published between January 2025 and June 2026. Sources include the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), the Office for National Statistics (ONS), the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) in partnership with the University of Essex, techUK, and independent consultancy benchmarks. Results: Active SME AI adoption rose from twenty-five per cent in 2024 to fifty-four per cent by early 2026, yet strategic deployment with defined business purpose remains at approximately sixteen per cent. Sectoral disparities are severe, with Information and Communication firms reporting adoption of forty-three to fifty-one per cent against six per cent in construction. Skills gaps (cited by over sixty per cent of firms), tool fragmentation, ROI uncertainty, and governance deficits are the principal barriers. An estimated £78 billion in economic value remains unrealised. Conclusion and policy recommendation: AI presents an unprecedented entrepreneurial opportunity and a corresponding project management challenge for UK SMEs. Government AI Adoption Hubs should embed formal project management frameworks alongside technical assistance, and SMEs should prioritise use-case-led deployment underpinned by clear governance, measurable key performance indicators, and workforce AI literacy investment. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence, Small and Medium Enterprises, United Kingdom, Entrepreneurship, Project Management, Digital Transformation

title: Vyapar AI - Voice-First Business Assistant for Small Enterprises
abstract: India has a large number of micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) over 63 million in total, almost all of which use manual processes and paper records for their day-to-day activities. Adoption of technologies is hindered by lack of digital literacy, cumbersome user interfaces, lack of adequate support for regional languages, and dependence on internet access. Vyapar AI tackles these problems by offering a voice-first, offline-capable mobile application for Android based on natural voice commands in Hinglish (Hindi + English) allowing owners of small businesses to handle their inventories, invoicing, client data, payment history, and business intelligence. The software combines React Native CLI frontend, Python FastAPI backend, and on-device speech recognition with Vosk engine, thus completely removing dependence on internet connectivity. Speech is analyzed with a deterministic rule-based NLP system, enabling prompt and predictable interactions without resorting to cloud-based APIs. Invoices can be shared and payment reminders sent directly from the application through deep linking for WhatsApp, thus avoiding use of external API services altogether. All business intelligence, such as sales summary, best-selling products, and stock shortages, is processed by the AI engine offline. This paper presents design considerations, architecture description, mathematical models, implementation details, and evaluation of features provided by Vyapar AI along with a comparison of closely-related applications and directions for further research.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Beyond maturity:the AI adoption navigator for manufacturing SMEs
abstract: Small- and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises face significant challenges in adopting Artificial Intelligence due to resource scarcity and a lack of tailored guidance. Existing artificial intelligence maturity models are frequently too abstract and biased. This research-in-progress addresses this gap by proposing the Artificial Intelligence Adoption Navigator, a conceptual framework specifically designed to evaluate AI adoption readiness small- and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises. Following the Design Science Research approach and utilizing the Technology-Organization Environment (TOE) framework, the proposed artifact deconstructs artificial intelligence adoption into granular, manageable micro-steps. A key innovation is the use of deterministic binary logic to replace subjective scales, mitigating self-assessment bias and providing actionable feedback. Preliminary validation through expert walkthroughs confirms the model's pragmatic alignment with the needs of small- and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises. This work provides a theoretical foundation of artificial intelligence for resource-constrained manufacturing entities.
venue: The UWS Academic Portal (University of the West of Scotland)

title: AI And Digital Technology: Catalysts for Sustainable Business Practices Among Small and Medium Business
abstract: This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence (AI) and digital technologies in advancing sustainable business practices (SBP) among small and medium enterprises (SMEs). The research adopts bibliometric analysis on data collected from the Scopus and Web of Science databases, covering publications from 2010–2024. Using the Biblioshiny (Bibliometrix R package) tool, an initial dataset of 586 documents was filtered resulting in 341 relevant documents for analysis. The findings reveal that the future of SBP lies in the adoption of AI and digital technologies. AI and digitalization enhance sustainable practices by improving resource utilisation, enabling decision-making based on data, and supporting predictive maintenance and waste reduction. However, SMEs face several hurdles to adoption, such as high costs of implementation, lack of technical expertise, shortage of skilled personnel and regulatory concerns. Some strategies suggested include better capacity building, phased technology adaptation, collaboration with stakeholders and partners, government incentives, and improved data infrastructure to facilitate adoption. The study lists some AI tools that is used by organisations globally in context of SBP. Future research may explore specific adoption models and collaborative digital ecosystems that enable SMEs to integrate AI and digital technologies, ensuring inclusive and scalable progress toward sustainable business development.
venue: IJARSAI International Journal of Advanced Research Scientific Analysis & Inferences

title: Service Science Framework for Frugal AI: A Design Science Approach for AI Adoption in SMEs
abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) face structural barriers to artificial intelligence (AI) adoption, including limited budgets, data scarcity, and skill gaps, that render dominant resource-intensive AI paradigms inaccessible. This paper proposes the Service Science Framework for Frugal AI (SSFFAI), a Design Science Research artifact that integrates frugal AI engineering with Service-Dominant Logic to support cost-effective AI adoption in SMEs. SSFFAI defines four interdependent dimensions: value, management, science, and technology that are linked through a Support-Use-Enable logic that connects strategic objectives, business service systems, and lightweight AI techniques to the creation of multidimensional value. A four-stage co-creation method operationalizes the framework into actionable implementation guidance. Three illustrative instantiations demonstrate its applicability across manufacturing, retail, and professional services contexts. Unlike descriptive adoption frameworks, SSFFAI provides prescriptive design knowledge that reframes SMEs as resource-integrating service systems capable of achieving sustainable AI-enabled innovation.
venue: Journal of the Association for Information Systems

title: THE EFFECT OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION ON AUDIT QUALITY IN AUDIT FIRMS
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology stands out as one of the latest game changers in the field of accounting and auditing profession (Kokina & Davenport, 2017; Sutton et al., 2016). with continued generation of large amounts of financial as well as non-financial data, the audit process faces challenges in delivering efficient and comprehensive audit results (Issa et al., 2016; International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board [IAASB], 2020). In response, firms in the audit industries are now incorporating Artificial Intelligence based technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, robotic process automation, predictive analytics, and big data analytics in order to deliver Higher efficiencies, strengthen fraud detection, risk assessment, and effective decision-making Process (Davenport & Ronanki, 2018; Deloitte, 2023; PwC, 2023).This study seeks to analyse the impact of Artificial Intelligence on audit quality within the audit firms using a qualitative research approach to review of existing literature and professional reports on the subject matter . from the analysis, it emerges that, Artificial Intelligence technologies improves audit quality in terms of increasing efficiency, accuracy, risk assessment and fraud detection, despite challenges related to high cost of adoption AI, cybersecurity risks, data privacy issues, algorithmic bias, and technical expertise (KPMG, 2023; EY, 2023; ICAEW, 2022). conclusion arrived at in Analysis that AI technology must work hand in hand with not in replacement of professional judgments, as the experience, ethical deliberations, and skepticism of auditors are essential for delivering high-quality audit results (IAASB, 2020; Sutton et al., 2016) (IAASB, 2020; Sutton et al., 2016).

title: Does digital tax administration reshape the labor skill premium? The role of artificial intelligence technology heterogeneity
The Lock-In of Family Equity, Patience in Ownership and Firms’ Artificial Intelligence Adoption
abstract: While artificial intelligence (AI) offers substantial opportunities for organizational transformation, family firms remain comparatively reluctant to adopt this technology. This study examines whether structural tools—formal family governance mechanisms that lock family equity into legally separate vehicles—can facilitate AI adoption in family firms. We theorize that structural tools institutionally stabilize family socioemotional wealth (SEW) by reducing restricted-SEW anxieties and enhancing extended-SEW, thereby increasing patience in ownership and encouraging long-term technological investment. Using data on Chinese listed family firms from 2008 to 2022, we find that firms employing structural tools exhibit significantly higher levels of AI adoption, and that this effect is mediated by increased ownership patience. A series of robustness tests, including instrumental variable analysis, parallel trends test, and the Heckman two-step method, support our hypothesis. Moreover, the positive effect of structural tools persists under conditions of crisis, political uncertainty, sanctions, and performance pressure. This suggests that structural tools constitute a family governance mechanism with enduring resilience. Our findings primarily contribute to the literatures on family governance by highlighting how ownership-level institutional arrangements can reshape family priorities and enable strategic investment in AI.

title: Adoption of Artificial Intelligence in Accounting Practices: A Study of Moroccan Accounting Firms
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has brought significant transformation to professional practice across various industries, and accounting is one of the most highly impacted professions. By automating time-consuming and routine tasks such as data entry, invoice processing, and bank reconciliations, AI allows accountants to divert their focus to higher value services. Such services include financial analysis, strategic advisory, and personalized customer service. As a result, AI improves not just efficiency and accuracy but also the quality of service and hence innovation and competitiveness in accounting business. In order to develop a more nuanced understanding of the extent and nature of AI adoption by accounting practices, a qualitative research was conducted with the help of structured interview guide. This research involved several Moroccan accounting firms and aimed to identify the level to which AI tools were being adopted in their operations. The research identified growing interest in AI, and some firms are already leveraging AI-based solutions to automate processes and improve customer experience. However, the adoption of AI is not uniform. Some businesses are fully engaged in digital transformation, while others are held back by barriers such as budget constraints, shortage of technical expertise, or uncertainly about the return on investment. The findings highlight the double reality of momentum and caution. They point to the need for more awareness, targeted training, and enabling policies to support AI adoption. Overall, the study highlights the transformative potential of AI in accounting, especially when coupled with a clear strategic intent and investment in change management.

title: The Architectural Foundation of Generative AI: A Patent Analysis of Google's Attention-Based Sequence Transduction Neural Networks (US 10,452,978 B2)
abstract: Purpose: To systematically examine the patent "Attention-Based Sequence Transduction Neural Networks" (US 10,452,978 B2) and evaluate its technological, strategic, and commercial significance as the foundational architecture of modern generative artificial intelligence. The study investigates how the patented invention replaces recurrence and convolution with self-attention mechanisms to achieve faster training, improved parallelization, and superior sequence-transduction accuracy. Furthermore, the article assesses the patent's innovation potential, business value, societal impact, and future opportunities through structured analytical frameworks, thereby contributing to knowledge creation in the domains of generative AI, natural language processing, and machine learning infrastructure. Methodology: This study adopts an exploratory qualitative research approach to systematically analyze the selected patent. Relevant data were collected from open-access sources, including Google Search, Google Patents, Google Scholar, and supplementary AI-assisted research tools, and were subsequently organized and interpreted according to the study objectives. Structured analytical frameworks such as SWOC and ABCDEF were applied to generate meaningful insights into the patent's technological, strategic, and commercial significance. Results & Analysis: The analysis reveals that the patent introduces a transformative encoder-decoder architecture built entirely on self-attention and multi-head attention mechanisms, eliminating the sequential bottleneck inherent in recurrent neural networks. The results indicate significant advantages in training speed, parallelization, translation accuracy, and scalability. However, challenges related to computational resource requirements, patent enforceability against widespread industry adoption, and the rapid commoditization of the underlying technique are also identified. Overall, the study demonstrates that the patent possesses extraordinary technological innovation, foundational commercial significance, and strategic relevance as the architectural bedrock of the entire generative AI industry. Originality/Value: The originality of this patent analysis lies in its examination of the single most consequential AI architecture patent of the past decade — the Transformer — through a structured scholarly lens rarely applied to foundational machine learning patents. The study adds scholarly value by demonstrating how a purely attention-based architecture transformed sequence-to-sequence learning and enabled the subsequent generative AI revolution. Furthermore, the patent offers significant technological, commercial, and societal value by underpinning translation systems, conversational AI, code generation, and multimodal foundation models worldwide. Type of Paper: Case Study-based Exploratory Research.
venue: Poornaprajna International Journal of Basic & Applied Sciences (PIJBAS)

title: AI-Powered Phishing in the Era of Generative AI: Emerging Risks, Business Impact, and Organizational Defense Strategies
authors: Dr S R Sundaravalli G Kokila Selva Kumari
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping cybersecurity by enabling both cyber defense and cyber offense. Phishing, one of the oldest cyber threats, has evolved dramatically through Generative AI and Large Language Models (LLMs), which allow attackers to craft personalized, grammatically correct, and context-aware phishing content at scale. AI-powered phishing increases the risk of credential theft, financial fraud, Business Email Compromise (BEC), ransomware, and data breaches, while conventional detection techniques struggle to keep pace. This study examines the evolution of phishing attacks, the role of Generative AI in cybercrime, the business impact of AI-driven attacks on organizations, and existing defense mechanisms, using a qualitative methodology based on secondary data. The findings show that AI has amplified attacker capabilities while simultaneously equipping organizations with powerful tools for threat detection, behavioral analysis, automated incident response, and predictive security. The study proposes the AI-SHIELD Framework, an integrated model combining AI-based detection, employee awareness, identity management, governance, incident response, and continuous monitoring. The research concludes that a proactive, AI-enabled, and governance-driven cybersecurity strategy is essential for organizations to withstand the next generation of phishing threats.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Governing Generative AI Across Financial Institutions: A Framework for Generative AI Risk Control
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is moving from general-purpose experimentation toward specialized applications across banking, capital markets, insurance, payments, and wealth management. Its main contribution is not limited to conversational interfaces. Modern generative systems can synthesize large document collections, extract information from unstructured data, generate software and analytical code, create scenario narratives, support research workflows, and coordinate multi-step tasks. These capabilities make generative AI especially relevant to finance, where decisions often depend on combining quantitative data with contracts, policies,filings, news, customer communications, and expert judgment. This paper presents an application-oriented view of generative AI in finance. It organizes potential uses around five capability patterns, including knowledge synthesis, content generation, analytical assistance, interaction, and workflow orchestration, and maps them to major financia functions. Representative applications include investment research, customer service, lending support, fraud investigation, financial reporting, operations automation, software development, and personalized financial guidance. The paper also discusses common technical architectures, such as retrieval-augmented generation, tool-using assistants, multimodal models, and agentic workflows, and identifies practical factors that shape business value. The resulting landscape provides a foundation for researchers and practitioners seeking to understand where generative AI may produce the greatest operational and analytical impact in financial services

title: Generative AI in higher education: efficiency, motivation and challenges in teaching business mathematics
abstract: This study explores the impact of applying ChatGPT-4, a generative artificial intelligence (AI) model, in the teaching of Business Mathematics. The research had a dual aim: to generate diverse problem sets to support teachers, and to enhance students’ critical thinking by involving them in the verification of AI-generated solutions. Conducted with 342 undergraduate students at the University of Debrecen, the experiment focused on differentiation tasks. ChatGPT-4 solved these with 94% accuracy, and the majority of students (90%) also performed well. Student feedback indicated that the approach was both useful and motivating. Cluster analysis identified three distinct learner groups – Self-Determined Enthusiasts, Duty-Bound, and Drifters – who differed significantly in their engagement with AI-based learning. While most students positively evaluated the use of ChatGPT-4, many also recognised its limitations and the need for critical reflection. The findings suggest that the conscious and pedagogically grounded integration of AI into mathematics education holds considerable potential. However, the development of critical awareness and the continued presence of human oversight remain essential to ensure meaningful learning outcomes. However, its effectiveness depends on ethical use, ongoing critical reflection, and the sustained pedagogical involvement of educators.

title: AI Literacy, Workforce Readiness, and Higher Education Transformation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy has emerged as a major challenge for higher education systems responding to workforce transformation, technological disruption, and evolving employability expectations. As AI increasingly reshapes labor markets worldwide, universities face growing pressure to prepare students for AI-enhanced professional environments requiring digital fluency, adaptability, and ethical reasoning. This mixed-methods study examined AI literacy and workforce readiness perceptions among Chinese higher education participants using survey data from 288 participants and interview data from 60 participants. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics, including Structural Equation Modeling (SEM), while qualitative interview data were analyzed through thematic analysis. The SEM results demonstrated that AI literacy positively influenced workforce readiness both directly and indirectly through confidence in using AI, ethical awareness, and institutional preparedness. Qualitative findings reinforced these relationships by highlighting participants' concerns regarding workforce anxiety, institutional readiness, ethical AI use, misinformation, and unequal technological access while emphasizing the importance of interdisciplinary AI literacy, workforce-connected learning, and curriculum modernization. Collectively, the findings suggest that higher education institutions must move beyond isolated technological adoption toward comprehensive digital competency ecosystems that strengthen workforce readiness, employability, and lifelong learning. Although derived from a Chinese educational context, the findings provide important implications for higher education reform and workforce policy development in the United States.
venue: International Journal of AI in Pedagogy Innovation and Learning Futures

title: Critical Mass, Board AI Literacy, and AI Adoption in Strategy, Risk, and Workforce Transformation
abstract: Corporate boards are increasingly expected to oversee firms’ adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in strategy, risk governance, and workforce transformation. Yet boards vary widely in whether investments in AI translate into meaningful strategic action. Drawing on critical mass theory and upper echelons theory, we develop and test a moderated mediation model that explains when and how board-level AI training and AI literacy shape firms’ strategic AI adoption. We theorize that AI training enhances boards’ collective AI literacy, which in turn enables more active engagement in AI-related strategic, risk, and workforce transformation. However, we argue that this indirect effect is contingent on whether the board reaches a critical mass of AI expertise. Using survey data based on 123 Canadian board directors from various organizations, we find support for a moderated mediation model, with effects concentrated in strategic engagement. Our findings highlight the importance of board-level AI training and collective AI literacy for the strategic governance of AI adoption.

title: AI LITERACY, HUMAN–AI COLLABORATION AND WORKFORCE EFFECTIVENESS: A COMPETENCY FRAMEWORK FOR SUSTAINABLE ORGANIZATIONAL PERFORMANCE
abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is fundamentally transforming organizational structures, workforce competencies, and decision-making processes across industries. As AI technologies become increasingly integrated into business operations, organizations require employees who possess not only technical AI competencies but also AI literacy, collaborative capabilities, and adaptive learning skills. Despite the growing body of research on AI adoption and digital transformation, limited attention has been devoted to understanding how AI literacy and human–AI collaboration jointly influence workforce effectiveness within sustainable organizational environments. This conceptual study develops an integrated competency framework that explains the relationships among AI literacy, AI competencies, human–AI collaboration, continuous learning capability, and workforce effectiveness. Drawing upon the Dynamic Capabilities Theory, Human Capital Theory, and the Technology–Organization–Environment framework, the study synthesizes recent interdisciplinary literature to identify the essential competencies required for future employees in AI-enabled organizations. The proposed framework suggests that AI literacy serves as the foundational capability facilitating effective collaboration between humans and intelligent systems. Human–AI collaboration subsequently enhances employee productivity, decision quality, innovation performance, and organizational resilience. Furthermore, ethical AI awareness and continuous learning are proposed as critical enabling factors supporting sustainable organizational performance. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled workforce development by integrating fragmented perspectives into a comprehensive conceptual model. Practical implications are provided for higher education institutions, organizational leaders, policymakers, and human resource professionals seeking to prepare employees for the evolving demands of Industry 5.0 and the intelligent digital economy.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Integrating AI Literacy into Adult Education Programmes for Sustainable Community Development and Workforce Preparedness in Obio/Akpo Local Government Area of Rivers State
abstract: The study examined integrating AI literacy into adult education programmes for sustainable community development and workforce preparedness in Obio/Akpo Local Government Area of Rivers State. Three (3) purposes, research questions and hypotheses respectively guided the study. The study adopted a descriptive survey research design. The population of the study comprised of 485 respondents, 72 instructors and 413 beneficiaries in the adult training center in Obio/Akpor Local Government Are
venue: Rivers State University Journal of Librarianship Information and Contemporary Studies (RSU-JOLICS)

title: AI for Biotech Futures: Connecting Biotech Companies and Educators to Shape an AI-Ready Workforce
abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly transforming biotechnology, with applications now spanning drug discovery, protein and molecule design, bioprocess optimisation, quality management, regulatory affairs, scientific writing and diagnostics. As biotechnology becomes increasingly data-driven and computational, graduates entering the sector will need to demonstrate not only subject knowledge, but also the ability to use AI tools effectively, ethically and critically. This white paper examines the emerging AI skills gap between biotechnology education and industry expectations. It identifies three key stakeholder groups: employers, universities and students. Each group has different expectations of AI use, but greater collaboration between them is needed to ensure that biotechnology graduates are prepared for an AI-enabled workforce. The paper highlights several challenges facing higher education. First, unequal access to AI tools risks creating an uneven playing field for students, particularly where subscription-based tools offer better performance than free versions. Second, AI has disrupted traditional assessment methods such as essays, lab reports, literature reviews and online exams, raising concerns about whether current assessments still measure genuine student learning. Third, the ethical use of AI remains unclear for many students and staff, especially in relation to academic integrity, AI declarations, hallucinated references and the limitations of AI detection tools. Finally, there is a subject-specific AI training gap, as many universities provide only general AI guidance rather than biotechnology-focused training. To address these challenges, the paper recommends that universities provide equitable access to appropriate AI tools for both students and staff. It also argues that assessments should be redesigned either to prevent inappropriate AI use or to encourage transparent and productive AI collaboration. Alternative assessment formats, such as bioprocess design dossiers, industrial case-study investigations, quality-by-design briefs, public-facing explainers and AI-supported data analysis tasks, may better reflect the skills required in biotechnology workplaces. The paper further recommends that AI ethics and academic integrity should be embedded into student training from the start of degree programmes. Students should be taught how to evaluate AI outputs, verify sources, recognise hallucinated references, declare AI use appropriately and understand the risks of over-reliance on AI-generated content. Staff should also receive structured training so that they can use AI confidently, redesign assessments and support students effectively. A two-level approach to AI skills development is proposed. All biotechnology students should receive basic AI literacy training, including prompt engineering, literature searching, writing support, revision, scientific image generation, data handling and critical evaluation of AI outputs. More advanced AI skills, such as coding, machine learning, AI model development, large dataset analysis and biotechnology-specific AI applications, should be embedded into specialist modules, practical classes and final-year projects. Overall, this white paper argues that universities must act quickly to embed AI skills into biotechnology education. By improving access to AI tools, redesigning assessments, strengthening ethical guidance and working more closely with industry, higher education can help close the AI skills gap and prepare graduates for responsible, effective and productive careers in the biotechnology sector.

title: Perspective Chapter: Educating Clinicians for AI-Driven Care and Surgery – Literacy, Human-Centered Design and the EU AI Act
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) evolves from passive decision-support tools to agentic clinical assistants – capable of drafting documentation, synthesizing complex cases, and automating surgical workflows – the educational requirements for clinicians are fundamentally changing. This transition represents a pivotal moment in medical history, akin to the introduction of medical imaging, yet the workforce remains largely unprepared for the shift from “human-in-the-loop” to “human-on-the-loop” interaction. This chapter addresses the critical gap between the rapid deployment of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) in medicine and the current lack of formal AI literacy in medical and surgical curricula. We propose a comprehensive framework for training the “agentic clinician”, built on three interdependent pillars: advanced technical literacy, human-centered design (HCD), and regulatory compliance under the new EU AI Act. Drawing on recent analyses and surveys of medical and dental students regarding trust, perceived roles, and preparedness, we outline a pragmatic curriculum that maps AI competencies onto existing clinical rotations. We then present a human-centered integration checklist for wards and operating rooms designed to mitigate risks such as, automation bias, hallucinations, and loss of situational awareness. Finally, the chapter operationalizes the EU AI Act by translating high-risk classification and postmarket monitoring obligations into concrete policies for hospitals and training programs. This roadmap is intended to empower educators and decision-makers to cultivate a workforce capable of safely supervising autonomous systems, ensuring that AI remains a tool for augmenting – rather than replacing – human clinical judgment.

title: Dynamic capabilities theory and human capital theory: building an AI-ready workforce for the future of work
abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how organizations operate, make decisions and manage talent. While many organizations are investing heavily in AI technologies, workforce readiness remains a major challenge. This study aims to explore how Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Human Capital Theory can help organizations build an AI-ready workforce capable of thriving in the future of work. Design/methodology/approach This conceptual study integrates insights from Dynamic Capabilities Theory, Human Capital Theory and emerging AI workforce literature to develop a practical framework for workforce readiness. Findings This study proposes that AI readiness is achieved when organizations combine adaptive organizational capabilities with continuous investments in employee development. Five key drivers are identified: AI literacy, continuous learning, workforce adaptability, future-focused talent management and leadership support. Originality/value This study bridges Dynamic Capabilities Theory and Human Capital Theory to explain workforce readiness in AI-enabled organizations and presents a practical roadmap for HR leaders navigating technological transformation.

title: AI Literacy in the Psychology Curriculum—Balancing Tradition and Innovation?: Comment on Robinson et al. (2026)
abstract: This paper explores the need to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) proficiency into undergraduate psychology education, building on the framework proposed by Robinson et al. Although AI presents both significant opportunities and societal risks, psychology majors seem to be well-positioned to address these challenges through their competencies in ethics, critical thinking, and the study of human behavior. AI literacy is essential for preparing graduates to navigate a rapidly changing workforce. By extending established curricular documents and guidelines, such as the American Psychological Association's Guidelines for the Undergraduate Psychology Major 3.0, institutions can enhance the relevance and value of psychology degrees. However, successfully integrating AI literacy into the existing psychology curriculum requires both practical pedagogical strategies and the consideration of the philosophical challenge of preserving the human-centered focus of psychology education.

title: Validation of the University of Florida AI Literacy Model for IT Skill Development in Saudi Higher Education
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Artificial intelligence (AI) literacy is increasingly essential in higher education for developing digital competencies, but its impact on IT skill acquisition remains underexplored in Arab contexts. Objectives To evaluate the effectiveness of the University of Florida (UF) AI Literacy Model in enhancing IT competencies among Saudi university students, aligning with Vision 2030's digital transformation goals, and to examine factors influencing skill retention and practical application. Methods In a randomized control‐group design, 60 students aged 18–22 were assigned to either the experimental group, which completed a 10‐session AI literacy intervention, or the control group, which followed traditional IT instruction. Pre‐ and post‐intervention achievement tests measured proficiency in navigation, file management, system customization, and troubleshooting. The mixed‐methods approach also incorporated surveys, interviews, and machine learning classifiers to analyse outcomes. Results The experimental group exhibited significantly greater improvements in IT skills, with large effect sizes. Machine learning analyses identified attendance and regular tool usage as key predictors of success. High‐engagement learners showed strong retention, with performance gains aligning with DigComp 2.2 standards. However, students' ethical awareness remained limited, with only 30% spontaneously raising privacy concerns. Conclusions This study provides the first empirical validation of the UF AI Literacy Model in an Arab higher‐education context. It offers evidence of both effectiveness and skill retention conditions, providing implementation insights for Gulf state educational contexts. Curricula should include regular AI tool practice and explicitly assess ethics (privacy, bias, and transparency). Institutions should implement graded ethical checkpoints to foster digital fluency and workforce readiness.

title: Generative AI and Information Management in Singapore SMEs: A Practical Framework for Adoption, Governance, and Workforce Readiness
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is changing how organisations create, retrieve, analyse, and use information. For small and medium-sized enterprises in Singapore, generative AI offers practical opportunities to improve productivity, customer engagement, knowledge management, marketing, data analysis, internal communication, and decision-making. However, successful adoption is not only a question of choosing the right AI tools. It is also an information management challenge involving data quality, workflow design, employee readiness, governance, privacy, human oversight, and evaluation. This working paper examines generative AI from the perspective of an AI practitioner working with business users and digital products. It proposes a practical framework for Singapore SMEs that want to adopt generative AI in a responsible and measurable way. The framework focuses on six areas: identifying business use cases, preparing information assets, designing human-AI workflows, building AI literacy, managing risks, and measuring outcomes. The Version 1.2 SME Practitioner Edition adds practical quick-start guidance, quick-win use cases, a 30-60-90 day adoption plan, sample prompt templates, a one-page AI usage policy template, and a simple results tracker for SMEs that want to save time and see measurable results quickly. The paper is written for SME leaders, educators, AI practitioners, trainers, information management professionals, and business teams seeking a practical introduction to generative AI adoption. It argues that SMEs should treat AI adoption as an organisational capability rather than a one-time technology purchase. When implemented thoughtfully, generative AI can help SMEs make better use of their information, reduce repetitive work, improve service quality, and strengthen workforce readiness for an AI-enabled economy.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Artificial Intelligence Literacy Among School Teachers in Sri Lanka: Measurement, Determinants, and Equity Implications for National AI Curriculum Readiness
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) is incorporated into national school curricula worldwide, the AI literacy of the teaching workforce has emerged as a decisive condition for effective and equitable implementation. Sri Lanka has begun integrating AI into its school information and communication technology (ICT) curriculum from the lower-secondary level, including a 2024 pilot establishing AI student societies in one hundred selected schools, yet the AI literacy of its teachers remains unmeasured. Existing national evidence is limited to the self-efficacy of ICT teachers. It does not assess AI literacy as a multidimensional competency, does not extend to the broader teaching workforce, and does not examine how AI literacy is distributed across the country's well-documented digital divides. This study addresses these gaps through three linked aims: to develop and validate a context-appropriate, trilingual instrument measuring teachers' AI literacy; to identify the demographic, professional, and institutional factors associated with that literacy; and to examine its equity implications across sector, province, gender, and school type. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design is proposed, combining a national cross-sectional survey of government-school teachers with validation analyses (exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, reliability estimation, and measurement invariance testing across the Sinhala, Tamil, and English versions) and a subsequent qualitative phase of interviews to explain observed patterns. The study is expected to deliver the first teacher AI literacy measure validated across all three of Sri Lanka's languages of instruction, a baseline national estimate for the government-school workforce, evidence on the correlates and equity patterning of teacher AI literacy, and policy-relevant guidance for the design of equitable teacher professional development in support of national AI curriculum readiness.

title: Integrating AI Chatbots and Blockchain Smart Contracts: Enhancing Fintech Accessibility for Low-Digital-Literacy Workers
abstract: Digital financial services powered by artificial intelligence (AI) and blockchain technology present transformative opportunities for workforce empowerment, yet vocational workers with limited digital literacy face significant adoption barriers. This study develops and validates an integrated framework combining AI-powered chatbots with blockchain-based smart contracts to enhance fintech accessibility for low-digital-literacy workers in Indonesia. Using sequential explanatory mixed-methods design, we analyzed data from 618 vocational workers across five Indonesian cities through structural equation modeling (SEM) and 12 focus group discussions with 86 participants. Results demonstrate that AI chatbot personalization (β=0.726, p<0.001) and smart contract automation (β=0.742, p<0.001) significantly enhance adoption, with the integrated model explaining 71.4% of adoption variance. AI chatbots reduce onboarding time by 67% through adaptive interfaces and contextual guidance, while smart contracts enable automated salary disbursement (85% efficiency gain), micro-lending decisions (72% approval accuracy), and transparent credential verification (94% accuracy). Individual digital capability (β=0.721), organizational infrastructure (β=0.586), and technical barrier mitigation (β=-0.445) emerged as critical determinants. Qualitative findings reveal three transformation pathways: automated financial processes, personalized learning journeys, and trustless verification systems. The framework provides evidence-based guidance for practitioners and policymakers implementing inclusive fintech systems that combine AI’s adaptive learning capabilities with blockchain’s transparency and automation benefits.
venue: Buana Information Technology and Computer Sciences (BIT and CS)

title: Cybersecurity for smart and resilient manufacturing and supply chains: A systematic review of the evolving knowledge base
abstract: Securing smart manufacturing increasingly requires a resilience-oriented cybersecurity perspective that extends beyond the factory floor to include digitally connected assets, operational dependencies, and supply-chain interfaces. In this paper, smart manufacturing refers to the digitally enabled production environment, resilience refers to the ability of that environment to anticipate, withstand, recover from, and adapt to cyber–physical disruption, and supply chains are treated as an extension of the same risk surface through which trust, traceability, software, components, and operational dependencies propagate. This paper synthesizes peer-reviewed literature and authoritative guidance to characterize threats, defenses, and operational gaps at the system level of manufacturing systems. Using a PRISMA-style protocol, we map evidence across hardware/firmware, software/data pipelines, and AI security; evaluate detection and response mechanisms (digital twins, anomaly/intrusion recognition, zero-trust patterns); and relate these to standards and sector profiles relevant to OT/IT interoperability. Building on the synthesis, we propose a six-pillar framework for cyber–physical resilience: (1) cyber–physical risk engineering design for secure manufacturing; (2) federated testbeds for verifiable trust and secure interoperability; (3) adaptive cyber–physical threat response; (4) risk-informed decision-making and cyber-risk communication; (5) adoption pathways and operational implementation; and (6) embedded cybersecurity culture and engineering literacy. The framework aligns technology, governance, and workforce levers to reduce downtime risk, improve recoverability, and support scalable deployment across heterogeneous assets and supply networks. We conclude with a research agenda that prioritizes traceability and verification, testbed-driven validation, quantification of cyber risk and value-at-risk, lifecycle management standards, and field evaluations, providing actionable steps to advance resilient, efficient, and sustainable manufacturing systems, anchored in verifiable evidence and practical validation.

title: Preparing Graduates for an AI-Driven Economy
abstract: Artificial intelligence is reshaping workforce demands, requiring higher education to redesign curricula that develop both technological competence and uniquely human skills. Integrating digital literacy, ethical reasoning, interdisciplinary learning, and lifelong learning prepares graduates to adapt to AI-driven workplaces while promoting responsible innovation. Curriculum innovation, supported by educational leadership and industry collaboration, is essential for producing future-ready graduates capable of thriving in an increasingly intelligent economy.

title: Preparing the Healthcare Workforce for Ethical Artificial Intelligence Adoption in Oman: An Ability–Motivation–Opportunity Perspective
abstract: HRMARS - This study examines workforce readiness for ethical AI adoption in Oman’s healthcare system and identifies human resource development strategies needed to support implementation. A qualitative interpretivist design was used. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 stakeholders from government, academia, industry, and civil society, selected through purposive and snowball sampling. The data were analysed thematically and interpreted through the Ability–Motivation–Opportunity (AMO) framework. The findings reveal four interconnected workforce challenges. First, ability deficits included limited AI literacy, insufficient data and digital skills, weak ethical literacy, and inadequate exposure to AI-supported clinical decision-making. Second, motivational barriers included fear of job displacement, low trust, concerns about professional autonomy, and uncertainty regarding accountability for AI-assisted decisions. Third, opportunity constraints included limited structured training, weak interdisciplinary learning, insufficient employee involvement in AI implementation, and unequal access to digital resources between urban and rural facilities. Fourth, dependence on foreign consultants restricted knowledge retention and the development of sustainable local capability. The study proposes an AMO-aligned human resource development agenda comprising competency-based training, scenario-based ethics education, participatory implementation, multidisciplinary AI teams, leadership development, and enforceable knowledge-transfer arrangements.
venue: International Journal of Academic Research in Business and Social Sciences

title: Mapping AI Across World in Education: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of National Policies and Government AI Readiness
Artificial Intelligence and Transversal Skills for Future Workforce: A Bibliometric Analysis of Research in Higher Education (2020–2025)
abstract: The rapid growth of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI technologies, is transforming higher education and redefining the competencies required for the future workforce. In this context, transversal skills such as critical thinking, collaboration, digital competence, and ethical reasoning are increasingly recognized as essential for engaging effectively with AI-driven environments. Despite growing scholarly attention to AI in education, the broader research landscape connecting transversal skills and AI in higher education remains insufficiently mapped. This study addresses this gap through a bibliometric analysis of 1,487 Scopus-indexed publications published between 2020 and 2025. Using Bibliometrix and VOSviewer, the analysis examines publication trends, collaboration patterns, leading countries and institutions, and the conceptual structure of the field. The findings reveal a rapidly expanding research landscape, particularly following the emergence of generative AI tools. AI literacy, digital competence, and critical thinking emerge as the most prominent competencies within the literature. The analysis also identifies five major research themes centered on curriculum transformation, pedagogical innovation, AI literacy and digital competence, educator capacity building, and professional readiness. Emerging topics such as metacognition, ethical reasoning, and workforce readiness suggest a growing shift toward human-centered competencies that support effective human–AI collaboration and prepare graduates for AI-driven future work environments.

title: WIP: Software Engineering Competencies in the Age of AI
abstract: A university education is meant to fully prepare graduates to enter and succeed in the workforce in their field. Accreditation bodies and professional organizations help to achieve this by publishing curriculum content, skills and competency models to outline the basics that universities must teach within a degree program. Although these curriculum guidelines and competency models are periodically updated to align university curricula with current industry needs, the needs of industry evolve rapidly and are often not properly reflected within the model, a situation which is occurring now with the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) use in industry. This paper reviews literature describing the AI needs within industry to motivate two new AI competencies, AI Literacy and AI development, within the Software Engineering Competency Model (SWECOM). This work then analyzes the industry needs described in the literature to propose the necessary skill areas for these new competencies.

title: EU AI Act Enforcement Begins in Two Days. ISO 42001 Is Not a Harmonised Standard. It Confers No Presumption of Conformity. Every Organisation That Certified to ISO 42001 to Demonstrate EU AI Act Compliance Has a Certification That Does Not Do What They Think It Does.
abstract: EU AI Act enforcement powers begin August 2 2026 with investigations orders and fines up to €35 million or 7 percent worldwide turnover. ISO/IEC 42001 published December 2023 is the world's first AI management system standard held by Microsoft PwC Canada Cornerstone and hundreds of others. ISO 42001 as of 2026 is not a harmonised standard under the EU AI Act and confers no presumption of conformity. Harmonised standard prEN 18286 developed by CEN-CENELEC JTC 21 entered public enquiry October 30 2025 - not listed in Official Journal. ISO 42001 is a management system standard specifying organisational processes not product-level technical controls. EU AI Act Articles 12 14 and 17 require product-level logging human oversight and quality management technical evidence. ISO 42001 does not specify what those product-level technical controls must contain. Constitutional command layer - cryptographic audit trails tamper-resistant override logs pre-execution gates - is the bridge that prEN 18286 will eventually specify.
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

title: Can AI Be Auditable?
abstract: Auditability is defined as the capacity of AI systems to be independently assessed for compliance with ethical, legal, and technical standards throughout their lifecycle. The chapter explores how auditability is being formalized through emerging regulatory frameworks, such as the EU AI Act, which mandate documentation, risk assessments, and governance structures. It analyzes the diverse challenges facing AI auditability, including technical opacity, inconsistent documentation practices, lack of standardized audit tools and metrics, and conflicting principles within existing responsible AI frameworks. The discussion highlights the need for clear guidelines, harmonized international regulations, and robust socio-technical methodologies to operationalize auditability at scale. The chapter concludes by emphasizing the importance of multi-stakeholder collaboration and auditor empowerment in building an effective AI audit ecosystem. It argues that auditability must be embedded in AI development practices and governance infrastructures to ensure that AI systems are not only functional but also ethically and legally aligned.

title: BEYOND COMPLIANCE: EMBEDDING ETHICS-BY-DESIGN IN ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE SYSTEMS UNDER THE EU AI ACT
abstract: This article explores the evolution of artificial intelligence governance in the European Union, focusing on the shift from regulatory compliance toward ethics-by-design. While the EU Artificial Intelligence Act establishes a comprehensive risk-based framework, the study argues that compliance alone is insufficient to address deeper ethical challenges related to human autonomy, dignity, fairness, and power asymmetries in algorithmic systems. The article conceptualizes ethics-by-design as a form of operational normativity that embeds ethical principles directly into the lifecycle of AI systems. It identifies key mechanisms for such integration, including ethical impact assessments, algorithmic auditing, transparency tools, and human oversight. At the same time, it highlights challenges such as translating abstract values into technical practices and avoiding superficial formalization. The study concludes that ethics-by-design is a necessary condition for the legitimacy of AI governance in the EU. By integrating ethical reasoning into system design, it becomes possible to bridge the gap between legal compliance and substantive justice, reinforcing a human-centric model of digital governance.

title: Inference as the defining criterion of AI: rethinking the EU AI Act
abstract: This article examines how inference operates as a legal and operational threshold in the EU Artificial Intelligence Act. It argues that a system's capacity to infer how to generate outputs, rather than simply executing predefined instructions, is the key criterion distinguishing AI from traditional automation. Tracing the evolution of the Act's definition of an ‘AI system’, the article shows how inference emerged as its core distinguishing concept, shaping both scope and regulatory purpose. Drawing on computational theory and safety-critical regulation, it proposes a problem-oriented framework for evaluating AI systems in legal contexts. Instead of relying on abstract or exhaustive definitions, this approach classifies AI systems by the problems they solve, the inference methods they employ, and the risks they pose. The framework accommodates hybrid systems, including neuro-symbolic and quantum-enhanced models, offering a more precise, technology-neutral basis for legal interpretation, compliance and enforcement under the AI Act.
