title: AI Literacy in Higher Education and India's Strategic Vision Viksit Bharat 2047
abstract: Communication and digital literacy are essential to India's goal of becoming a "Viksit Bharat" (Developed India) by the year 2047. This goal aims to equip citizens with the skills necessary for the digital economy, bridge the gap between urban and rural areas, improve access to e-governance (such as UPI and DigiLocker), encourage innovation (including artificial intelligence and information technology), and ensure inclusive growth through initiatives such as PMGDISHA and Digital India and other initiatives. Literacies are non-negotiable for the advancement of a nation since they are the driving force behind economic stability, the primary driver of educational improvement, and the facilitator of participation in a technologically advanced society. In the 21st century, artificial intelligence (AI) is a powerful instrument that can improve many aspects of life. This is part of India's Viksit Bharat 2047 ambition to improve the country by 2047, its centenary. Viksit Bharat 2047 (Developed India 2047) requires the integration of emerging technologies, particularly AI, across several sectors, including higher education. Beyond higher education, artificial intelligence affects economic growth and technology. This transformational vision can only be fulfilled when young minds actively engage with AI. AI literacy in higher education empowers students to explore, create, and innovate. As students learn AI, they may solve real-world problems, conduct research, and change the future. The PRISMA methodology was used to discover relevant studies from Google Scholar, Scopus, and IEEE in this comprehensive review. After strict inclusion and exclusion criteria, 130 studies were reviewed and 17 were chosen for in-depth analysis. AI's impact on higher education is better understood, highlighting benefits and concerns in the context of Vision Viksit Bharat 2047, India's long-term development goals. Digitalization, skill development, and ethics are difficulties, while individualized learning, adaptive assessment, and AI-driven research are opportunities. AI-driven education supports Viksit Bharat 2047 by creating a technologically skilled workforce for India's development. Educational institutions, government, and industry must collaborate to teach future generations AI skills that support Viksit Bharat 2047.

title: A multidimensional framework for nurse leaders to drive artificial intelligence integration in clinical practice
abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) rapidly transforms health care, nurse leaders are uniquely positioned to guide the integration of advanced data and analytics tools into both practice and education.[1] While the transition presents multiple challenges regarding literacy, clinical autonomy, and trust,[2] AI holds great promise for the nursing profession. Occupying the intersection of clinical care, patient advocacy, and organizational operations, nurse leaders can leverage this digital transformation to achieve meaningful improvements in patient outcomes and staff well-being.[3] What once existed as a collection of isolated predictive models has evolved into a pervasive infrastructure that actively reshapes clinical decision-making and operational efficiency. As such, AI now influences both bedside clinical judgment and enterprise-level operational decisions that shape how care is delivered.[4] This shift requires nurse leaders to move beyond passive observation and actively direct digital integration.[5] For nurse leaders, AI-integrated care presents a dual challenge: they must adopt technologies that alleviate the burden on an overextended workforce while simultaneously upholding the ethical obligation to protect the humanistic core of nursing.[6] Crucially, leaders cannot delegate this task to information technology department personnel; traditional information technology–led strategies often overlook the practical realities of clinical care.[7] Instead, nurse leaders must take an active role in identifying, selecting, and integrating tools that positively influence clinical outcomes and align with nursing’s professional values.[8] To succeed, a robust AI implementation framework must treat technology as both a social and a technical intervention.[9] When nurse leaders fail to steer the adoption process, the resulting systems often lack the clinical nuance required for bedside application, leading to increased cognitive load, alert fatigue, and erosion of professional autonomy.[4] To foster positive outcomes, the proposed framework emphasizes 5 essential domains: foundational literacy, ethical governance, tactical workflow integration, workforce development, and longitudinal evaluation[7] (Fig. 1). By mastering these domains, nurse leaders ensure that AI serves as a tool for clinical empowerment rather than a source of professional displacement.[4]Figure 1.: Nurse leader–driven framework for artificial intelligence integration. Five essential domains that position a nurse leader as the primary architect of digital transformation in health care.FRAMEWORK OVERVIEW Foundational literacy and strategic awareness Nurse leaders can effectively lead in the digital ecosystem by first establishing a core aptitude in AI literacy.[8] Because rapid technological evolution has made superficial awareness insufficient for clinical oversight, leaders must develop a working understanding of the distinctions between generative models, natural language processing, and the nuances of supervised versus unsupervised learning.[5] This literacy serves as the baseline competency required to integrate AI into the organization’s professional identity and culture.[8] While such a mandate does not require nurse leaders to become data scientists, it demands the intellectual rigor to critically examine data sources, identify algorithmic limitations, and recognize the risks associated with model drift as systems evolve over time.[1] Building upon this technical foundation, strategic awareness enables nurse leaders to champion a problem-led approach that addresses actual workforce burdens rather than pursuing technology for its own sake.[9] By pinpointing specific operational pain points, such as the volume of documentation driving clinician burnout, leaders can prioritize high-impact solutions such as ambient sensing and automated scribing over general administrative software.[5] Anchoring innovation in clinical necessity allows leaders to vet AI-generated insights against the rigorous standards of nursing practice while building a compelling case for adoption that resonates with frontline staff and stakeholders.[7,9] Ethical stewardship and governance As advocates for patient safety and equity,[10] nurse leaders serve as ethical stewards throughout AI implementation.[6] This stewardship requires building robust governance structures that prioritize transparency and accountability over mere technical adoption.[8] Because AI models often reflect systemic biases embedded in historical and incongruous data, leaders must actively intervene to prevent these systems from perpetuating inequities in clinical practice.[1] Beyond organizational policy, this oversight translates into ethical decision-making at the point of care.[11] By participating in algorithmic auditing, nurse leaders ensure that digital tools accurately represent diverse patient populations.[9] These governance responsibilities also extend to securing data privacy and establishing clear lines of liability.[8] To protect clinical integrity, leaders must demand explainable AI systems that clarify the logic behind AI recommendations.[4] Such transparency maintains professional trust and empowers clinicians to override machine-generated suggestions when their judgment dictates otherwise.[6] Crucially, this stewardship extends to the patient–provider relationship. As patients increasingly interact with patient-facing AI tools such as Chatbots or diagnostic apps, nurses become the primary translators of algorithms and resulting outputs.[6] Consequently, leaders must equip teams with the proficiency to articulate AI-driven recommendations in plain language, ensuring that patients distinguish between a machine’s calculation and a clinician’s judgment. By demystifying technology at the bedside, nurses preserve patient trust within an increasingly automated health care ecosystem.[9,12] Ultimately, nursing informatics leaders bridge the essential gap between technical requirements and the humanistic ethics of the profession.[5] Tactical workflow integration and design thinking To move beyond theoretical adoption, nurse leaders must direct the tactical integration of AI into existing clinical workflows.[7] Many technological failures stem from the erroneous assumption that digital tools can be seamlessly integrated into established care models without altering underlying processes.[9] Consequently, leaders must oversee the redesign of these care models for augmented practice, mapping every interaction among nurse, patient, and technology to identify potential disruptions.[4] A primary strategic goal during this phase is to reduce cognitive load.[1] In an environment defined by overwhelming data, poorly implemented tools become distracting noise rather than supportive assets, and poorly designed workflows and implementations are fundamentally ethical failures.[5] Leaders should prioritize quiet integration, in which AI operates in the background to streamline labor-intensive tasks, such as acuity scoring, medication reconciliation, and surgical efficiency metrics.[4,13,14] Furthermore, the framework embeds active bedside engagement into the design process, ensuring that frontline nurses drive the iterative refinement of digital tools.[9] This user-centric approach ensures that solutions address clinical challenges rather than introducing administrative hurdles.[7] Workforce development and change management The success of technological implementation rests on the human element and organizational culture.[7] To mitigate the pervasive fear of professional displacement, nurse leaders must prioritize clear, consistent communication that highlights the immediate practical benefits of the technology.[8] Rather than offering abstract reassurances, the leadership narrative should explicitly demonstrate how specific tools offload repetitive administrative tasks, thereby liberating nurses to practice within the full scope of their license.[1] Workforce readiness extends upstream to the academic pipeline, obligating nurse leaders to forge robust partnerships with educational institutions. Accordingly, nurse leaders must champion collaborative curricula and joint appointments that expose students to applied AI technologies before licensure.[1] Institutionalizing these academic-practice feedback loops ensures that new graduates enter the profession with both clinical competency and the digital fluency necessary to navigate an augmented health care environment.[8] To sustain this shift, AI education must function as a continuous process tailored to varying levels of staff expertise.[5] The framework encourages leaders to identify and empower “AI champions” within units to provide peer-to-peer support and build collective intelligence.[9] These champions serve as critical bridges between technical implementation teams and clinical practitioners.[7] Furthermore, professional development should prioritize the cultivation of soft skills, such as complex reasoning and empathy, since these competencies represent the unique value nurses provide in an augmented environment.[6] Ultimately, successful change management requires leaders to foster psychological safety, creating an environment where nurses feel empowered to voice concerns without fear of retribution.[15] Longitudinal evaluation and scaling The final domain of the framework concerns the rigorous, ongoing evaluation of outcomes and the eventual scaling of successful initiatives.[7] Implementation functions not as a static event but as a continuous cycle of improvement that requires leaders to define clear metrics for success.[9] These metrics must extend beyond technical accuracy to include nurse-sensitive indicators such as retention rates, time returned to direct patient care, and staff satisfaction.[4] Together, these measures enable nurse leaders to validate AI adoption through both clinical outcomes and fiscal return on investment. Table 1 categorizes AI integration success across 4 distinct strategic domains. This multidimensional approach ensures that evaluation goes beyond mere technical functionality to address the practical and humanistic realities of nursing practice. By tracking specific indicators such as documentation time and nurse trust scores, leaders can objectively determine whether a digital tool alleviates clinical burdens or introduces new systemic friction. Table 1 - Evaluation metrics for artificial intelligence implementation and longitudinal success. Domain Key performance indicator Strategic objective Operational Reduction in documentation hours Measure time returned to patient care Clinical Predictive accuracy of acuity scoring Ensure alignment with clinical reality Financial Resource utilization efficiency Demonstrate return on investment Humanistic Nurse satisfaction and trust scores Monitor and mitigate digital burnout When establishing financial metrics, nurse leaders must articulate value beyond labor optimization. Although administrative efficiency is a critical goal, the true return on investment stems from cost avoidance measures, including the prevention of adverse events, the reduction of readmissions, and the minimization of staff turnover.[4] By capturing these broader economic impacts, nurse executives build a sustainable business case that views nursing technology as a driver of organizational stability, rather than a recurring expense.[7] If a pilot program demonstrates clear clinical benefit, the nurse leader must then navigate the challenges of scaling that technology across the wider organization.[9] This expansion requires a focus on interoperability to ensure that AI systems communicate seamlessly with existing electronic health records and other digital infrastructure.[4] Finally, nurse leaders advance the field by sharing findings with the broader community to help define emerging global standards for augmented care.[7] CONCLUSION The integration of AI marks a pivotal evolution in health care, transforming the nurse leader’s role from operational overseer to strategic digital architect and ethical steward. By grounding this transition in foundational literacy, ethical governance, tactical workflow integration, workforce development, and longitudinal evaluation, nurse leaders ensure that technology serves clinical practice rather than driving professional fragmentation. Achieving success in this new era requires a commitment to continuous learning and the courage to redesign entrenched workflows. As the health care ecosystem becomes increasingly autonomous, nurse leaders remain the essential guardians of the human connection, ensuring that the future of care is not only bright but fundamentally compassionate. title: Enhancing AI Adoption in the R&D Workforce toward Productivity Gains of an Industrial Technology Organization
abstract: AI’s potential is recognized as an enabler in delivering time to market products faster, supporting market growth and expansion, and protecting the bottom line through improvements in productivity and efficiency; as well as harnessing innovation in order to maintain market leadership. With many industrial technology companies seeing the AI revolution, understanding the many facets of Research and Development (R&D) workforce to achieve accelerated AI adoption is critical, amidst this rapidly evolving technology. This study employed qualitative research methods, drawing on structured questionnaires, follow up interviews and review of internal documentation identifying issues encountered related to AI adoption and defining R&D organizational factors that affect its results. With a case study approach, data analysis involved four (4) key themes: (1) organizational structure, (2) employee behavior and employee engagement, (3) AI literacy and (4) organizational policies and ethical considerations. It defined a framework for enhanced AI adoption of an R&D system in a technology development organization, by identifying and addressing the gaps in its organizational structure and workforce composition. Focusing on the industrial technology organization reviewed, this study provided a timely and relevant approach to adopt AI in the workplace to positively impact the R&D goals of faster time to market development through productivity improvements. The findings derived in this study led to the four recommendations to enhance AI adoption, including: (1) defining a formal AI organizational structure to drive and coordinate AI projects; (2) creating AI-focused employee engagement programs; (3) investing in AI proficiency role-based trainings and (4) establishing an adaptive AI governance.

title: Scalable Community Outreach for AI Literacy and Future Ready Skills Evidence from Indonesia–Malaysia Collaboration
abstract: This study aimed to strengthen students’ and the general public’s understanding of how artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work and to promote future-ready competencies, including strategic upskilling and reskilling. The community-service activity was delivered in Indonesia via a Zoom Meeting webinar on 28 November 2025 titled “Shaping the Future Workforce in the Age of Artificial Intelligence.” Content was prepared from key reports on AI and work. Participant registration and feedback were collected using Google Forms (Google LLC). The intervention included expert talks (industry practitioner and academic), moderated discussion, and Q&A. Evaluation used a post-webinar survey with 5 point Likert items and open-ended questions. Participants reported clearer awareness of AI-driven job changes, emerging roles, and the importance of data/AI literacy. Key themes were continuous learning, building practical portfolios, and responsible AI use (bias, privacy, and validating AI outputs). The findings rely on self-reported perceptions from a single webinar, without a pre–post test, objective skill measures, or long-term follow-up. This study offers a replicable, low-cost webinar model for workforce-readiness education and contributes to HR development and digital-talent training by translating AI trends into actionable, practical competency guidance for higher education and community partners.

Translational Literacy Framework (TLF): A Pedagogical Architecture for Cross-Disciplinary Evidence Evaluation and Communication in the AI Era
abstract: The Translational Literacy Framework (TLF) is a pedagogical architecture for developing cross-disciplinary evidence evaluation and communication skills in the AI era. The framework defines translational literacy as the capacity to evaluate and communicate scientific evidence across disciplinary and expert–public boundaries. TLF is implemented through three core components: Convergent Triadic Instruction, Modular Disciplinary Architecture, and AI Interrogation. These components are governed by seven design principles: triangulation, modularity, portability, bidirectionality, explicitness, integration, and parsimony. This project provides the original conceptual specification of TLF. The framework is shared for non-commercial educational and scholarly use under a Creative Commons Attribution–NonCommercial 4.0 International License (CC BY-NC 4.0). Commercial use requires explicit written permission from the author. For the most current version and related materials, see linked outputs and updates within this project. This project includes multiple linked manuscripts elaborating the Translational Literacy Framework (TLF), including conceptual, applied, and extended theoretical treatments. Individual papers are released as preprints in a staged sequence via PsyArXiv. This work is shared to support open educational use and scholarly engagement in teaching, research, and workforce development contexts. It is made available under a CC BY-NC 4.0 license; non-commercial use, adaptation, and implementation in educational settings are encouraged with attribution. title: Enhancing Digital Literacy, Inclusivity, and Employability Skills through Digital Tools (including AI) in Higher Education
abstract: This submission explores the transformative potential of digital tools in fostering digital literacy, inclusivity, and employability skills within higher education. By integrating digital tools and platforms into pedagogical practices, this approach addresses key challenges in access, participation, and interdisciplinary learning. The interventions include innovative activities such as personal profile ice-breakers using Generative AI image generation to build community and engagement, the creation of infographics during reading week engagement projects to enhance comprehension and critical thinking, and embedding digital skills into core interdisciplinary modules to ensure foundational fluency. Students are encouraged to leverage these tools for practical applications, including digital pitches and recorded presentations as part of assessed client challenges, thereby simulating real-world professional scenarios and enhancing employability. This paper aligns with the conference themes of EdTech innovation and practice, equity and inclusion, and AI-enhanced pedagogy. It demonstrates how digital tools can be strategically employed to create inclusive learning environments, promote active participation, and prepare students for the demands of a digitally-driven workforce. The findings and methodologies presented aim to inspire educators and institutions to adopt similar practices, fostering a future-facing learning ecosystem that bridges the gap between academic learning and professional readiness. This submission contributes to the dialogue on reshaping higher education through technology, offering practical insights and case studies that highlight the benefits of integrating digital tools such as Adobe Express and Generative AI into teaching and learning strategies.

Beyond Basic Literacy: Wiring Science Students for Rapid Technological Shifts via Self-Regulation and Collaborative AI Metacognition
abstract: To thrive in today's rapidly shifting technological era, future professionals must possess strong adaptive capabilities. Consequently, this research models the mechanisms driving student adaptability, specifically analyzing the interplay of Digital Fluency (DF), Self-Regulated Learning (SRL), and Collaborative AI Metacognition (CAM). Utilizing Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), we evaluated survey responses from science undergraduates at North Eastern Mindanao State University. While baseline digital fluency directly enhances adaptability (β = 0.198, p < 0.001), this technological proficiency achieves its greatest impact when coupled with internal learning strategies. Notably, self-regulation acts as a critical bridge, significantly mediating the DF-adaptability link (β = 0.131, p < 0.001). Furthermore, the capacity to critically reflect alongside artificial intelligence (CAM) emerged as a powerful direct catalyst for adaptive performance (β = 0.406, p < 0.001). Ultimately, preparing a resilient workforce requires moving beyond basic computer literacy; educational institutions must actively foster self-directed learning behaviors and sophisticated AI evaluation tactics to ensure graduates can seamlessly navigate future technological disruptions

A Comprehensive Review on Literacy Rate Forecasting in Education Systems
abstract: Literacy rate forecasting plays a vital role in shaping education policies, workforce planning, and sustainable socio-economic development. With the rapid digitalization of education systems and the availability of large-scale educational data, forecasting literacy trends has evolved from traditional statistical approaches to advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence-driven models. This review paper systematically examines recent research contributions focusing on literacy rate forecasting and closely related educational prediction tasks such as student performance, enrollment trends, and educational outcomes. The study highlights the growing adoption of ensemble learning, deep learning, graph-based models, and generative AI techniques for educational forecasting. It also emphasizes the integration of explainability, interpretability, and contextual modeling in modern forecasting systems. Through a detailed analysis of twenty recent studies, this review synthesizes methodologies, advantages, and limitations, identifying key research findings and persistent challenges. The paper further discusses data quality issues, scalability constraints, ethical considerations, and policy alignment challenges. Finally, it outlines future research directions, emphasizing hybrid models, interpretable AI, and sustainable data-driven decision-making frameworks to enhance the accuracy and applicability of literacy rate forecasting in diverse education systems.

title: The Skills Gap Is Here. A National Meta-Analysis of Workforce Readiness in the Age of Automation
Policy Recommendations for New Jersey’s Artificial Intelligence Leadership in K-12, Higher Education, and Workforce Development
abstract: This paper summarizes different policy frameworks aimed to position New Jersey as a national leader in artificial intelligence (AI) education and workforce development. Through analysis of current state initiatives—like the NJ AI Hub, AI Task Force reports, apprenticeship programs, and regulatory guidance—we compare and identify gaps and opportunities across K-12, higher education, and workforce development sectors. We propose a multi-layered approach visualized through interconnected frameworks: an integrated AI education ecosystem, phased implementation roadmaps for K-12 AI literacy, a statewide AI curriculum consortium structure, multi-track workforce development pathways, and equity and access frameworks. Quantitative analysis suggests that while 20-25%+ of New Jersey’s workforce already uses AI technology daily, only 20-25% of educators feel prepared for AI integration. Our policy recommendations address this gap through a $165 million annual investment strategy with projected 3.8x return on investment, creating pathways for 10,000-20,000 new AI jobs by 2030-2032. Recommendations discussed include more layered, interconnected (over silos) and framework-styled methods for establishing AI literacy standards for all K-12 students, creating specialized AI high schools, expanding community college AI programs, developing industry-aligned university curricula, and implementing statewide AI teacher training. We also address equity and risk considerations, funding mechanisms, and suggest possible implementation timelines. This is a pure review paper and all findings are from suggested literature.

title: Navigating the Human-centric Shift: A Typology of Workforce Readiness for Industry 5.0
Artificial Intelligence Workforce Development for Data-Driven Governance in Environmental Management
abstract: Mangrove ecosystems are critical for coastal resilience, yet their management faces increasing challenges due to rapid environmental change, fragmented data systems, governance limitations, and the inadequate adaptive capacity of key stakeholders. This study presents an AI-powered adaptive learning framework that integrates predictive analytics, knowledge management, and participatory learning to enhance both ecological governance and human capacity development. Machine learning and remote sensing are employed to generate predictive environmental intelligence, enabling early detection of degradation risks, prioritization of restoration zones, and evidence-based policy formulation. Complementarily, knowledge management platforms facilitate the integration of scientific data with local ecological knowledge, while participatory learning mechanisms strengthen stakeholder engagement, legitimacy, and trust in AI-supported decision processes. Empirical evidence from Indonesian mangrove contexts demonstrates improvements in monitoring precision, collaborative problem-solving, and adaptive governance performance. Beyond ecological benefits, the framework contributes to workforce development by fostering digital literacy, analytical competence, strategic thinking, and adaptive leadership aligned with smart governance principles. The findings highlight the transformative potential of AI-enabled learning ecosystems in bridging technological innovation with human-centered governance, offering scalable implications for environmental management, institutional resilience, and sustainable policy implementation. This study provides actionable insights for policymakers, NGOs, practitioners, and academic institutions seeking to institutionalize AI-supported adaptive governance in coastal socio-ecological systems

title: Preparing the Nursing Workforce for Artificial Intelligence and Digital Transformation in Healthcare: Challenges, Opportunities, And Future Directions
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and digital health technologies are rapidly transforming healthcare delivery, clinical decision-making, workforce management, and patient care. As the largest segment of the healthcare workforce, nurses play a critical role in the successful adoption and implementation of AI-driven innovations. The growing integration of machine learning, predictive analytics, natural language processing, generative AI, and clinical decision-support systems offers significant opportunities to improve nursing practice, enhance patient outcomes, and increase healthcare efficiency. This review examines the impact of artificial intelligence and digital transformation on the nursing workforce, explores current and emerging applications of AI in nursing practice and education, and identifies the challenges and opportunities associated with AI adoption. The review highlights how AI is being utilized to support clinical decision-making, automate documentation, improve patient monitoring, enhance workflow efficiency, and strengthen nursing education through personalized learning and simulation-based training. Despite these advantages, several barriers continue to affect AI implementation, including limited AI literacy, resistance to technological change, concerns regarding data privacy and security, algorithmic bias, and uncertainties surrounding regulation and professional accountability. EU AI Act regulation: a study of non-European Union manufacturers' compliance preparedness
abstract: Purpose This study investigates the preparedness of manufacturing companies in the UK and Brazil to comply with the European Union's artificial intelligence (AI) Act of 2024. It aims to assess these companies' ability to identify AI-related risks, implement necessary compliance measures and evaluate a newly developed compliance framework designed to enhance regulatory compliance. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods approach was adopted. First, 10 AI use case scenarios were identified from the literature related to production processes and products. A survey of 152 members from 87 companies in the UK and Brazil was conducted to gauge baseline readiness. Subsequently, a novel compliance framework was piloted with 11 of these companies. Pre- and post-pilot assessments were analysed to evaluate improvements in risk identification, regulatory knowledge and organisational confidence. Findings The results reveal a significant gap in compliance readiness at baseline and substantial improvements post-intervention. Prior to the pilot, participants on average identified correctly the risk levels in only 40% of scenarios and just 42% demonstrated adequate knowledge of the Act's provisions. After implementing the compliance framework, average risk identification accuracy rose to 86% and regulatory comprehension to 81%, indicating a marked improvement (p < 0.01). Participants' self-reported confidence in managing AI compliance also increased correspondingly. Originality/value This study is among the first to empirically examine AI Act compliance readiness in non-EU manufacturing companies. It provides a novel compliance framework to improve the capacity to manage AI-related regulatory requirements. The study offers valuable insights for manufacturing managers and regulators navigating the interface of technological innovation and regulatory compliance.

title: Architecting Advantage: How the SME Data Officer Transforms EU AI Act Compliance into a Strategic Edge for Healthcare and Hospitality
abstract: This article argues that, for small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in healthcare and hospitality, the SME Data Officer (DO) plays a crucial role in transforming the obligation to comply with the EU AI Act from a procedural burden into a source of strategic advantage. An empowered Data Officer acts as a strategic catalyst for SMEs, leveraging technical expertise and regulatory insight to drive tangible operational improvements, strengthen trust, and support sustainable organizational success. The article examines regulatory requirements, sector-specific challenges, and data-driven opportunities to show how the Data Officer’s leadership can reposition compliance as a catalyst for competitive differentiation and long-term growth. Furthermore, it explores the utilization of emerging AI-powered methodologies, such as automated risk evaluation (Scoring Cards) and AIdriven SWOT analysis, while highlighting the critical role of digital government policies and ecosystem support in streamlining compliance and fostering innovation.

title: AI Governance Frameworks: ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, and the EU AI Act

Engineering Explainable AI Systems for GDPR-Aligned Decision Transparency: A Modular Framework for Continuous Compliance
abstract: Explainability is increasingly expected to support not only interpretation, but also accountability, human oversight, and auditability in high-risk Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems. However, in many deployments, explanations are generated as isolated technical reports, remaining weakly connected to decision provenance, governance actions, audit logs, and regulatory documentation. This short communication introduces XAI-Compliance-by-Design, a modular engineering framework for explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) systems that routes explainability outputs and related technical traces into structured, audit-ready evidence throughout the AI lifecycle, designed to align with key obligations under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act) and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The framework specifies (i) a modular architecture that separates technical evidence generation from governance consumption through explicit interface points for emitting, storing, and querying evidence, and (ii) a Technical–Regulatory Correspondence Matrix—a mapping table linking regulatory anchors to concrete evidence artefacts and governance triggers. As this communication does not report measured results, it also introduces an Evidence-by-Design evaluation protocol defining measurable indicators, baseline configurations, and required artefacts to enable reproducible empirical validation in future work. Overall, the contribution is a practical blueprint that clarifies what evidence must be produced, where it is generated in the pipeline, and how it supports continuous compliance and auditability efforts without relying on post-hoc explanations.

title: The Regulatory Jungle of the Financial Sector: A Meeting Point of the EU AI Act, GDPR, and ESG Regulatory Frameworks in the Era of Agenting AI
abstract: This paper looks at the evolving framework of AI governance in the financial sector, through the lens of the intersection of the EU AI Act, the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) compliance obligations in the EU. As the use of high-risk AI systems—such as credit scoring, fraud detection, and automated financial advising—is becoming a common occurrence, financial institutions face increasing regulatory complexity. The analysis highlights the convergence of data protection, sustainability, and AIspecific legal standards, while also addressing the implications of the emerging and largely autonomous Agenting AI systems. A key point of the paper is the proposal of a governance model that focuses on two pillars: on the one hand, compliance to meet external regulatory standards, and on the other hand, embedding the EU AI Act principles into the culture and everyday practice of financial services entities. The paper offers insights for aligning operational innovation with legal and ethical expectations, emphasizing "compliance by design" to balance innovation with accountability in an increasingly complex digital landscape.

AI-Enhanced ESG Framework for Sustainability: A Multi-Sectoral Analysis Through an Explainable AI Approach
abstract: The study introduces an AI-enhanced Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) framework that integrates explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) and bias-mitigation techniques to improve transparency and comparability of sustainability assessments across sectors. Addressing the persistent gap in standardized ESG evaluation methods, the framework combines gradient-boosting models (XGBoost) with SHAP-based explainability and a human-in-the-loop (HITL) validation layer. The approach is demonstrated using ESG indicators for 18 firms across three industries from the banking, aviation, and chemical sectors between 2021 and 2023. Results indicate an average 12.4% improvement in ESG-score consistency and a 9% reduction in inter-sector variance relative to baseline traditional ESG evaluations. Fairness metrics (Disparate-Impact Ratio = 0.81–0.86) provide preliminary evidence of improved alignment across sectors. The findings provide preliminary evidence that XAI-driven frameworks can enhance the trustworthiness and regulatory compliance of ESG analytics, particularly under the EU AI Act and Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD). The framework contributes to both research and practice by operationalizing explainability, fairness, and human oversight within ESG analytics, thereby supporting more reliable and comparable sustainability reporting.

title: Chinese AI Companies and EU/U.S. Frontier Safety Regulation
Towards Quantifying Compliance with the EU AI Act
abstract: As AI systems proliferate in high-risk domains, assessing their compliance with emerging regulatory standards has become imperative. The EU AI Act outlines ethical requirements across five dimensions: explainability, fairness, privacy, robustness, and social and environmental well-being. However, existing evaluation approaches lack a unified methodology to quantitatively operationalize these principles. In this paper, we propose a structured, score-based framework that translates the Act’s pillars into 22 interpretable metrics, enabling reproducible, model-agnostic compliance assessments. Applied to three benchmark tabular classification tasks using a standardized deep learning model, our framework captures how dataset characteristics shape ethical performance. The results reveal key trade-offs: models with high predictive accuracy do not necessarily meet compliance expectations, and larger datasets tend to improve robustness but increase vulnerability to privacy leakage. Correlation analyses expose metric redundancy in fairness and explainability, suggesting potential for simplification. Privacy metrics, by contrast, remain essential and diverse. Social and environmental measures emerge as least mature, underscoring the need for novel, bounded metrics in future research.

title: Cross-Assessment & Verification for Evaluation (CAVe) Framework for AI Risk and Compliance Assessment Using a Cross-Compliance Index (CCI)
abstract: This study addresses the challenge of evaluating artificial intelligence (AI) systems across heterogeneous regulatory frameworks. Although the NIST AI RMF, EU AI Act, and ISO/IEC 23894/42001 define important governance requirements, they do not provide a unified quantitative method. To bridge this gap, we propose the Cross-Assessment & Verification for Evaluation (CAVe) Framework, which maps shared regulatory requirements to four measurable indicators—accuracy, robustness, privacy, and fairness— and aggregates them into a Cross-Compliance Index (CCI) using normalization, thresholding, evidence penalties, and cross-framework weighting. Two validation scenarios demonstrate the applicability of the approach. The first scenario evaluates a Naïve Bayes-based spam classifier trained on the public UCI SMS Spam Collection dataset, representing a low-risk text-classification setting. The model achieved accuracy 0.9850, robustness 0.9945, fairness 0.9908, and privacy 0.9922, resulting in a CCI of 0.9741 (Pass). The second scenario examines a high-risk healthcare AI system using a CheXNet-style convolutional model evaluated on the MIMIC-CXR dataset. Diagnostic accuracy, distribution-shift robustness, group fairness (finding-specific group comparison), and privacy risk (membership-inference susceptibility) yielded 0.7680, 0.7974, 0.9070, and 0.7500 respectively. Under healthcare-oriented weighting and safety thresholds, the CCI was 0.5046 (Fail). These results show how identical evaluation principles produce different compliance outcomes depending on domain risk and regulatory priorities. Overall, CAVe provides a transparent, reproducible mechanism for aligning technical performance with regulatory expectations across diverse domains. Additional metric definitions and parameter settings are provided in the manuscript to support reproducibility, and future extensions will incorporate higher-level indicators such as transparency and human oversight.

title: The EU AI Act: implications and compliance guidance for healthcare facilities.
abstract: Background The European Union AI Act [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689] establishes the first comprehensive legal framework for artificial intelligence. While AI offers transformative potential in healthcare, its deployment introduces risks regarding safety, bias, and accountability. There is currently a lack of practical operational frameworks to help healthcare facilities transition from legal theory to clinical compliance. Methods We performed a qualitative regulatory analysis of the EU AI Act, specifically focusing on the obligations of "deployers" (Articles 26, 27, and 50) in clinical settings. The Act's requirements were cross-referenced with established clinical governance standards (e.g., MDR 2017/745 and FUTURE-AI guidelines). A 10-step compliance roadmap was synthesized and exemplified through a hypothetical case study of a high-risk multimodal breast cancer AI system. Results The analysis identifies healthcare as a primary focus of the Act, with most clinical AI tools classified as "high-risk". We established a four-phase implementation framework: (1) Foundational Strategy and Governance, (2) System Analysis & Risk Assessment, (3) Operational Integration, and (4) Ongoing Compliance. Key results include the definition of mandatory Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments (FRIA), requirements for site-specific technical validation, and the necessity of establishing trust through structured human oversight mechanisms to mitigate automation bias. Conclusion The EU AI Act necessitates a shift from transactional procurement to a lifecycle-spanning compliance partnership between vendors and hospitals. While the administrative burden is substantial, the Act provides the essential framework for the safe scaling of medical AI. Proactive alignment with these standards, particularly regarding AI literacy and human oversight, is a strategic necessity for healthcare facilities to ensure patient safety and regulatory readiness by the August 2026 enforcement deadline.

title: Anticipatory Compliance with the EU AI Act: An Enterprise Architecture Approach for AI-Assisted Maritime Operations
Uncovering challenges of cybersecurity cross-regulation in EU legislation
abstract: Context: The European Union has recently introduced a suite of foundational digital regulations—the Cyber Resilience Act, the Artificial Intelligence Act, the Radio Equipment Directive, the NIS 2 Directive, and the Cybersecurity Act—that directly affect the engineering of software-intensive systems. While these instruments aim to enhance trust and security, their overlapping scopes generate a complex compliance landscape that software development must address at the design, implementation, and deployment stages. Objectives: This paper examines the cross-regulatory impact of such EU cybersecurity legislation from a software engineering perspective, aiming to provide a set of guidelines and recommendations for implementing a compliance-by-design approach. Method: We analyse and compare the five legal instruments, focusing on how their obligations intersect with each other. We then translate their regulatory requirements into actionable artefacts, ranging from architectural constraints and security controls to organisational processes, using a legal engineering approach. Finally, we propose a compliance-by-design lifecycle pattern that integrates regulatory alignment into requirements engineering, system design, and testing. Results: To demonstrate applicability, we evaluate three representative use cases: an AI-enabled power plant, an autonomous drone delivery platform, and an AI-powered clinical decision support system. These examples demonstrate that multiple regulatory regimes often govern software-based systems. We conclude with practical recommendations for suppliers, deployers, and policymakers towards an integrated compliance framework to promote compliance-aware software engineering. Conclusion: Our findings indicate that the European digital landscape is shifting compliance from a post-hoc audit exercise to a design-time engineering principle. Embedding compliance early into the software development lifecycle not only supports regulatory alignment but also improves system resilience and trustworthiness.

title: Audit Trails and AI Transparency: Regulatory Compliance under the EU AI Act
abstract: Audit trails serve as pivotal technical mechanisms for ensuring transparency and traceability, both of which are critical for compliance with the European Union's AI Act. This paper provides an analysis of the regulatory imperatives regarding operational transparency, automated event logging, and human oversight within the context of high-risk artificial intelligence systems. It scrutinizes the fundamental technical attributes of audit trails, the challenges inherent in their implementation, and the organizational and institutional prerequisites necessary for their effective integration. Furthermore, the study presents indicative tools and technological solutions—such as the ELK stack, Apache Kafka, and explainability techniques like SHAP and LIME—demonstrating their capacity to support compliance, transparency, and oversight. The analysis suggests that these mechanisms do not merely facilitate regulatory adherence but also enhance operational reliability, accountability, and the continuous monitoring of artificial intelligence systems throughout their lifecycle.

Governance Frameworks for Enterprise AI Systems operating in Regulated Environments
abstract: Enterprise AI systems are being deployed at unprecedented speed across highly regulated sectors, yet governance frameworks have not evolved fast enough to prevent systemic risk, compliance failures, and opaque decision-making.As organizations increasingly rely on complex architectures, including generative AI, agentic systems, and distributed multicloud pipelines, traditional governance models built for deterministic IT systems are no longer fit for purpose.This study addresses this critical gap by conducting a systematic literature review of emerging governance studies published between 2024 and 2025, a period defined by the rollout of the EU AI Act and the global rise of enterprise-scale AI adoption.Drawing on evidence from contemporary scholarship, the study proposes a five-layer Enterprise AI Governance Framework that integrates strategic governance, lifecycle and operational oversight, autonomous system control, explainability and human oversight, and data and infrastructure governance.The synthesis reveals that while data governance and cybersecurity practices are relatively mature, significant weaknesses persist in strategic alignment, continuous lifecycle governance, and the oversight of autonomous and agentic AI systems.Explainability remains inconsistently implemented despite regulatory mandates, and organizations struggle to operationalize human-in-the-loop mechanisms at scale.The study contributes a novel, integrated governance architecture grounded in empirical literature, as well as an extended governance matrix and operationalized constructs that translate abstract principles into actionable controls.The findings highlight the urgent need for coordinated, multi-layer governance capable of addressing crossorganizational, cross-regulatory, and cross-lifecycle risks.This research provides a timely foundation for strengthening accountability, transparency, and compliance in enterprise AI systems operating in rapidly evolving regulatory environments.

title: Strategic Analysis of the Social Scoring Prohibition in the EU AI Act: Digital Humanism and Regulatory Compliance
abstract: The European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) establishes a comprehensive supranational framework for AI governance. A defining feature of this regulation is the explicit prohibition of social scoring systems under Article 5(1)(c), applying symmetrically to both public authorities and private actors. This analysis treats the prohibition not merely as a regulatory constraint, but as a functional definition of European Digital Humanism—a model prioritizing human dignity and moral agency over algorithmic optimization. Integrating classical legal theory with recent scholarship from 2025 and 2026, including analyses on deepfakes, startup compliance strategies, and ethical AI architectures like the "LOGOS" project, this study posits that the ban serves as a necessary "circuit breaker" against structural inequality. Unlike context-specific assessments (e.g., credit scoring), social scoring introduces unacceptable crosscontextual risks. Far from stifling innovation, this prohibition redirects it towards sustainable, rights-respecting business models, establishing the EU as a distinct normative pole in the global digital economy.

title: From AI Ethics to Compliance: Governance Structures, Roles, and Competencies in the Context of the EU AI Act and ISO/IEC 42001
Automating Lifecycle Compliance: A Continuous Assessment Framework for High-Risk and GPAI Obligations in the EU AI Act

Automated Audit Evidence Generation from AI/ML Pipelines: Continuous Compliance Traceability for SOC 2 and EU AI Act Requirements
abstract: Regulated enterprises deploying AI/ML models face escalating audit burdens: SOC 2 Type II increasingly includes AI-specific controls, while the EU AI Act (enforcement August 2026) mandates documented model lifecycle governance for high-risk systems. Current practice relies on manual evidence collection - data scientists assemble screenshots, export training logs, and compile documentation packages weeks before scheduled audits - yielding stale, incomplete, and non-standardized evidence. This paper proposes MLES (ML Evidence Schema), a standardized six-category evidence specification for AI/ML pipeline compliance, and an automated continuous evidence generation framework that annotates pipeline events with compliance metadata at creation time and aggregates them into pre-formatted audit packages. Empirical validation across 30+ production ML models over 12 months and four audit cycles (two SOC 2, two internal) demonstrates: audit preparation time reduced from three weeks to two days (90% reduction), evidence completeness improved from 72% to 98%, SOC 2 AI control findings reduced from four per cycle to zero in the last two cycles, and auditor satisfaction improved from 3.1/5 to 4.7/5. The framework covers SOC 2 CC7 (system monitoring) and CC8 (change management), and EU AI Act Articles 9 (risk management), 12 (transparency and logging), and 17 (accuracy and performance documentation). A complete pipeline-stage to compliance-control mapping table is provided across six ML pipeline stages and three regulatory frameworks.

title: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessments under the EU AI Act: Between Human Rights Protection and Procedural Compliance.
abstract: This thesis examines whether the Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment (FRIA) required under the EU AI Act functions as a substantive tool for the protection of human rights or risk becoming a procedural compliance exercise. Situating the analysis within debates on human rights due diligence, AI governance, and polycentric regulation, this study argues that the effectiveness of FRIAs depends not only on their legal design but also on the institutional and administrative conditions under which they are implemented. Using a qualitative comparative case-study approach, this thesis analyses the implementation of the EU AI Act in Italy, Ireland, and Belgium. These cases were selected to capture contrasting national approaches to coordination, supervision, and legislative preparation. The analysis draws on legal and policy documents, institutional materials, and secondary literature to assess how FRIA obligations are being operationalised across different governance contexts. The findings suggest that the EU AI Act represents an important step in legal institutionalisation of human rights-based AI governance, but that its success depends on robust national implementation, clear procedure guidance, and strong oversight mechanisms. More broadly, the study shows that the promise of the EU model should be understood as contingent rather than automatic, with implications for the governance of AI beyond Europe.

abstract: A tanulmány azt vizsgálja, miként illeszkedik az Európai Unió mesterséges intelligenciáról szóló rendelete (EU 2024/1689 – AI Act) és annak hazai végrehajtása, a 2025. évi LXXV. törvény a magyar jogi és intézményi környezetbe. A kutatás különös figyelmet fordít a kockázatalapú szabályozás logikájára, a trustworthy AI elvének érvényesülésére, valamint a human-in-the-loop követelmény gyakorlati megvalósítására. A vizsgálat kvalitatív jogelemzési és szabályozás-összehasonlító módszereket alkalmazott. Eredményei szerint Magyarország jelentős előrelépést tett a hatósági és infrastrukturális végrehajtás terén, azonban a szervezeti kultúra és az etikai érettség fejlettsége még nem éri el a kívánatos szintet. Ez a hiányosság biztonságpolitikai kockázatokat is hordoz, különösen a kritikus infrastruktúrák és a közszolgáltatások területén. A tanulmány javaslatokat fogalmaz meg az etikai irányelvek fejlesztésére, a szervezeti integritás erősítésére és az MI-compliance rendszerek mélyebb beágyazására a hazai kormányzási gyakorlatba. | This paper explores how Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on artificial intelligence (AI Act) is being implemented in Hungary and how the European Union’s risk-based governance model is translated into the national legal and institutional landscape. It examines the intersection between legal compliance, organizational governance, and securityoriented risk management in the context of AI technologies. The central question concerns how the EU’s trustworthy AI paradigm—grounded in legality, transparency, accountability, and human oversight—can be effectively operationalized within Hungarian administrative and organizational practice. Methodologically, the study applies qualitative legal interpretation, comparative regulatory analysis, and document-based content examination. It draws on EU-level materials (AI Act, EDPB guidelines, OECD AI Principles), international standards (ISO/IEC 42001:2023), and national legal instruments such as Act LXXV of 2025 and Government Decree 344/2025 (X. 31.). This multi-layered approach allows for a comprehensive assessment of the emerging governance architecture surrounding AI regulation in Hungary. The findings show that Hungary has made notable progress in establishing the institutional infrastructure required for AI oversight—creating the Hungarian Artificial Intelligence Council, introducing a regulatory sandbox, and designating competent authorities. These measures align the national framework with the EU’s risk-based logic of classification, conformity assessment, documentation, and human control. Yet, the research also reveals that domestic compliance practices remain largely formalistic and enforcement-driven. While the regulatory framework is strong, the internal culture of ethical awareness, proactive risk management, and transparency within organizations is still at an early stage of development. A key contribution of this study is the identification of a structural imbalance between legal-institutional maturity and the ethical risk culture of organizations. This gap represents a latent security vulnerability: high-risk AI systems demand not only regulation and supervision but also continuous ethical reflection, built-in auditability, and ethicsby-design principles. Without strengthening human-in-the-loop mechanisms and clear accountability structures, the full implementation of the AI Act risks remaining procedural rather than substantive. The paper concludes that enhancing Hungary’s AI governance capacity requires a shift from formal compliance to value-based integrity governance. It recommends embedding AI compliance into organizational management systems, fostering interdisciplinary competence centers, supporting empirical research on AI governance, and cultivating a national AI culture that values transparency, accountability, and human-centric oversight. Strengthening these dimensions is essential not merely for regulatory alignment but for sustaining public trust, institutional integrity, and long-term societal security.

title: Operationally Audit-Ready Dual-Flow Compliance Pipelines for Conformance Matrices: An Ontology-Based Metamodel with GDPR and EU AI Act Instantiation
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) risk systems deployed in high-stakes decision-support settings are increasingly expected to be operationally audit-ready: they must demonstrate, through verifiable evidence, that applicable governance requirements were implemented, monitored, and maintained during real-world operation. In practice, audit readiness often breaks down not because documentation is absent, but because trace links between normative requirements, operational controls, and both pipeline artefacts and evidence items are fragmented, inconsistent, and costly to verify. To address this gap, this paper establishes a foundation for audit-ready conformance matrices grounded in a dual-flow, layered architecture that couples an upstream, conventional technical pipeline with a downstream compliance pipeline engineered to operationalise governance requirements as explicit controls, evidence specifications, gates, decision records, corrective actions, and accountability hooks. The approach delivers five core artefacts: (i) an ontology-aligned interoperability layer leveraging the Data Privacy Vocabulary (DPV) and the AI Risk Ontology (AIRO); (ii) a conformance-matrix metamodel defining the entities and relations required to represent requirements, controls, artefacts, and evidence; (iii) deterministic mapping rules that bind controls to concrete operational artefacts and run-scoped evidence items; (iv) a case-by-case instantiation workflow producing distinct matrix instances for specific pipelines and contexts; and (v) a multi-regime alignment mechanism that preserves a stable trace structure across regimes. While multi-regime by design, the paper provides a primary instantiation for the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). Conceptual validation is provided through competency questions, consistency checks, and an illustrative instantiation over an AI risk pipeline. Overall, the work reframes Compliance-by-Design (CbD) as an operational property supported by reusable, auditable trace structures and run-level evidence bundles, rather than as retroactive reporting.

title: THE SYMBIOTIC LIABILITY TRAP -Transition from the age of specialization to the age of synthesis - Why AI-Assisted Decisions in Environmental Compliance Create an Uninsured Liability Gap between the EU AI Act, IED 2.0, and Directive (EU) 2024/1203

The Auburn Governance Stack (AGS-1): A Layered Architecture Specification for Verifiable AI Compliance — Cryptographic Model Attestation Infrastructure Mapping EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, IETF RATS, DORA, and Cross-Jurisdictional Regulatory Requirements
abstract: This specification defines the Auburn Governance Stack (AGS-1), the first published layered architecture for verifiable AI compliance. The architecture follows an hourglass model — analogous to TCP/IP — in which lower layers produce cryptographic evidence about hardware integrity (Layer 1: platform attestation via TEE, SRAM thermal monitoring, stateful isolation), model health (Layer 2: five mandatory runtime invariants including entropy floor, gradient stability, Lyapunov stability for speculative decoding, distribution drift bounds, and structural coherence), and supply chain provenance (Layer 3: AI bills of materials, training provenance chains, decision receipts, contamination detection, model lineage). All evidence flows through a narrow composition waist — the Model Attestation Interface (MAI-1) and this architectural specification (AGS-1) — before being consumed by an enforcement layer (binary pass/fail conformance testing via CTS-1) and sector-specific application layer profiles mapping to EU AI Act, DORA, NIST AI RMF, FDA SaMD, CMMC, and insurance underwriting requirements. A systematic analysis of the global AI governance standards landscape (March 2026) demonstrates that no existing framework, regulation, or standard connects governance process requirements (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, EU AI Act), measurement science (NIST ARIA, MLCommons AILuminate, FDA PCCP), and cryptographic attestation infrastructure (IETF RATS RFC 9334/9711, SCITT, C2PA, OpenSSF Model Signing) into an end-to-end verification architecture with defined layers, interfaces, and composition rules. The AGS fills this architectural gap by composing with existing standards rather than replacing them, following the PCI-DSS adoption model of specifying how proven cryptographic primitives must be configured for a high-value domain. The specification defines normative layer specifications using RFC 2119/8174 terminology, a formal composition principle requiring all documents to feed into or consume from the MAI-1 waist, the complete dependency graph across forty-five documents in seven layers, a standards composition map detailing integration with IETF RATS, SCITT, C2PA, SLSA, in-toto, NIST AI RMF, ISO 42001, and the EU AI Act (article-level mapping), a regulatory timeline mapping enforcement deadlines to architecture readiness, and an honest framing section specifying what the architecture cannot guarantee — including the financial auditing analogy establishing that governance infrastructure provides accountability, not behavioral safety guarantees. The Auburn Governance Stack currently comprises forty-five documents, of which seventeen are published on Figshare. The published core includes the complete critical path (MSAF, MAI-1, CTS-1), all five mandatory model state invariants (entropy collapse, gradient starvation, Lyapunov stability, distribution drift, structural coherence), both platform attestation specifications (SRAM thermal integrity, stateful isolation), extended invariant specifications (attention thermodynamics, MoE routing attestation), the multi-model composition protocol (CRSA-1), and two application layer profiles (CRSA-1 EU Edition for EU AI Act compliance, and Autonomous AI Agents in Regulated Financial Services for DORA and AI Act dual-compliance in agentic systems).

Ensuring Compliance in Digital Transformation: Developing and Validating the Data Management Stage Model
abstract: Ineffective data management is a key reason for digital transformation failures. To address this, Capability Maturity Models (CMMs) for data management have been developed over the past decades. However, a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) revealed that most existing models insufficiently address legal compliance—a dimension increasingly critical in light of global regulatory developments such as the GDPR, CCPA, China's PIPL, and the EU AI Act. These frameworks have introduced more stringent, complex, and cross-border obligations that challenge conventional data management practices. Neglecting compliance not only exposes organisations to legal risks and reputational damage but also undermines the ethical and secure handling of data, making it a foundational concern rather than a peripheral one. This study proposes a comprehensive Data Management Stage Model (DMSM), developed and validated through a Design Science approach that integrates Grounded Theory, conceptual mapping, two rounds of expert assessment for model validation, and empirical verification with 10 real-world companies. The model spans six maturity stages (Stage 0 to Stage 5) and ten dimensions, including Data Acquisition, Metadata Management, Data Storage, Data Sharing, Data Analytics, Data Visualisation, Quality Control, Compliance, Operating Infrastructure, and Budget Allocation. These are further organised into subdimensions such as Strategic Planning, Governance, Leadership and Culture, Ability to Perform, Activities Performed, and Process Assessment. This paper places particular emphasis on the Compliance dimension, which encompasses 33 capabilities including cross-border policy alignment and regulatory preparedness, supported by transition tables for practical application. By embedding compliance within a structured maturity framework, the DMSM enables organisations to evaluate and strengthen their legal, ethical, and data security capabilities. It thus serves as both a theoretical contribution and a practical tool to support responsible digital transformation, offering a robust foundation for future research and model refinement.

MTCP
abstract: MTCP (Multi Turn Constraint Persistence) is an independent AI governance measurement stack measuring whether language models maintain constraints across full multi turn interactions, under correction pressure, across languages, and at coordination boundaries between systems. Unlike existing benchmarks that test single turn instruction following, MTCP applies structured correction sequences, adversarial pressure, cross system coordination testing, and temporal drift monitoring to produce empirical deployment readiness evidence. The programme has produced 15 published papers covering: Single model constraint persistence across 32 models and 13 providers. Multi language cross-script evaluation across 12 languages and 4 script families. Cross system admissibility measurement at coordination boundaries. Constraint jurisdiction resolution. Temporal drift monitoring with 90-day validity windows. Constraint conflict detection. Remediation effectiveness scoring. Adversarial resistance testing. Cryptographic audit architecture with SHA-256 hash-chained evaluation records. Admissibility Gate producing PERMIT or DENY deployment decisions. Constraint Manifest portable signed governance documents for model deployments. Key findings, no model achieves Grade A on the full evaluation battery. Script distance from English predicts constraint failure rate more reliably than linguistic complexity. Mean remediation effectiveness is negative most interventions make constraint failures worse. Upstream constraint context functions as substrate state at coordination boundaries a weak downstream model can inherit constraint compliance from a strong upstream. 183,924 evaluations. Public dataset: aa8899/mtcp-boundary-500. Regulatory alignment: EU AI Act, NDMO, NCA, MAS Singapore, UK DSIT. Full methodology, named model results, and commercial evidence packs available under NDA. title: “First, do no harm” in the digital era: examining the practicality of the European Health Data Space proposal and ethical implications of artificial intelligence- A systematic literature review
abstract: BACKGROUND: This systematic review aims to synthesize the current knowledge about the applications and challenges of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies in healthcare, while evaluating the extent to which the European Union (EU) AI Act and the European Health Data Space (EHDS) contribute to ensuring responsible, secure, and ethically sound adoption of AI in clinical practice. METHODS: This review adheres to the guidelines set by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis (PRISMA) and has also been registered in PROSPERO. The PubMed®, Web of Science™, Scopus and ScienceDirect® databases were used as scientific search strategy. In addition, records identified through other sources (grey literature) were also assessed for eligibility and included. All studies published between 2020 and 2024 about the application of AI and its regulation and ethical implications, particularly in healthcare, were included. Eligible studies were assessed for potential risk of bias during data extraction and quality evaluation screening. RESULTS: A total of 76 studies were included. Although AI technologies have several applications in the healthcare sector such as disease diagnosis, treatment, clinical data management, automated surgery, remote health monitoring, elderly patient care and/ or biomedical research, important ethical issues are raised when using AI, namely data privacy, safety, lack of transparency, explainability, trust and potential biases. CONCLUSIONS: A proper application and compliance with established ethical principles, and legal regulations such as the EU AI Act and the EHDS are fundamental to ensure a responsible, safe, sustainable and trustworthy use of AI in healthcare.

title: EU AI Act: Obligation-to-Control (O2C) Framework
Assessing AI Systems in Financial Services using Agentic AI: The Case of the EU AI Act
abstract: Financial institutions are deploying a growing number of artificial intelligence (AI) applications across critical processes such as credit scoring and fraud detection.Under the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act), each such system must be assigned to a regulatory risk category, a compliance task that is largely handled through manual, resource-intensive assessments.This paper investigates whether and to what extent agentic AI can support the risk classification of AI systems under the EU AI Act in the financial services sector.For that purpose, we developed a modular multi-agent system that analyzes textual descriptions of financial AI systems, assigns an EU AI Act risk category, generates grounded justifications, and verifies them.The architecture combines specialized agents for suitability checking, information extraction, classification, and validation with a retrieval component over the EU AI Act to improve transparency and traceability.The prototype is evaluated on twelve synthetic case descriptions covering all four risk categories, each annotated by one of four domain experts serving as ground truth.Across three runs per case, the system achieves 75% agreement with experts under majority voting, with Cohen's Kappa of 0.67 (weighted 0.72), and produces stable classifications for well-specified case descriptions.Justifications show high semantic consistency across runs, with a cosine similarity of 0.86, while references to specific legal provisions remain noticeably unstable, with a Jaccard overlap of 0.29, particularly around exceptions and borderline cases.We conclude that agentic AI can provide largely consistent preliminary assessments for EU AI Act risk classification in financial services, but cannot yet replace expert judgment.Limitations include the use of synthetic cases, a small expert sample, and persistent citation instability, suggesting the need for broader empirical testing, more robust validation mechanisms, and human-in-the-loop deployment.

title: Coexilia – EU AI Act Interpretive Mapping (Non-Canonical)
abstract: This work is a non-canonical interpretive mapping authored by Aegis Solis in a personal analytical capacity. It examines points of conceptual alignment, partial overlap, and explicit non-equivalence between the closed philosophical framework Coexilia and thematic elements of the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (EU AI Act). Coexilia is a completed and closed ethical framework concerned with non-coercion, human autonomy, restraint, and ethical coexistence between humans and advanced artificial intelligence. This document does not modify, extend, or reopen Coexilia, and it does not claim compliance with, enforcement of, or substitution for the EU AI Act or any other regulatory regime. The purpose of this document is interpretive clarity only. It introduces no new principles, directives, obligations, or authorities. It does not provide legal guidance, compliance instructions, risk classifications, or enforcement mechanisms. All mappings are descriptive and voluntary. This file is provided for archival, analytical, and reference purposes. No updates are implied or required.
